event.title: Advance Your Research Skills with REAP – Apply by September 15
event.description:
Dear Cornell Life Sciences Researchers,

 

The Weill Institute for Cell and Molecular Biology is pleased to announce that the REAP application portal is now open. Applications will be accepted through September 15, 2026.

 

As scientific technologies continue to advance rapidly, the Research Expertise Advancement Program (REAP) supports Cornell life sciences laboratories in staying current with emerging tools and methods in cell and molecular biology. REAP provides full or partial funding (up to $3,000) for faculty, graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers to attend technology-focused workshops or courses, with the expectation that participants will share the acquired expertise with the broader Cornell community.

 

For program details and to apply, visit: https://wicmb.cornell.edu/reap/

 

Kind regards,
Weill Institute for Cell and Molecular Biology

event.title: America at 250: Focus on George Washington
event.location: Michael T. Sillerman '68 Rotunda, Rare and Manuscript Collections
event.location_name: Michael T. Sillerman '68 Rotunda, Rare and Manuscript Collections
event.address: 2B Carl A. Kroch Library, Cornell University Ithaca, NY 14853
event.description:
Cornell University Library’s Division of Rare and Manuscript Collections commemorates the 250th anniversary of the American Declaration of Independence (1776–2026) with an exhibition of rare books, letters, and documents on the life of George Washington.

These highlights of the collection reflect the interests of Cornell’s first president, Andrew Dickson White, who had a fascination with both American history and book collecting. The acquisition of rare materials relating to Washington and his era formed an integral part of White’s educational vision. Despite subsequent transformations in the discipline, White’s principle remains resonant: collecting, displaying, and teaching with rare books, autographs, signatures, and portraits make history tangible and alive.

event.title: ENCROACH: An Exhibition Exploring Privacy and Exposure in High Density Housing
event.room_number: In front of Goldwyn Smith Hall
event.description:
ENCROACH is an outdoor exhibition by the Housing Innovation Lab, which explores the tensions of privacy in high-density housing, where space is scarce, and boundaries are constantly contested.

A sequence of fragmented spaces reveals disjointed views — bodies without faces, views that are never simply given but must be physically negotiated — exposing the compromises of dense living, where seeing and being seen are never fully in your control. Wrapped in a reflective skin, the structure blurs inside and outside, and the line between watching and being watched begins to dissolve.

The Housing Innovation Lab (HiLab) explores the intersections of environmental, societal, and well-being concerns linked to housing and investigates synergies between building performance and quality of life across scales.

The Housing Innovation Lab is directed by Lecturer and Housing Innovation Research Fellow Katharina Kral.

This project is supported by the Cornell Council for the Arts and the Dean’s Professional Development Fund.

event.title: Just Ocean and Coastal Futures Conference
event.description: The Just Ocean and Coastal Futures Conference brings together future-oriented scholars at all career stages who integrate reparative frameworks into coastal and ocean studies. The purpose of the conference is to share and produce knowledge while imagining, designing, and supporting strategic action. Over three days of individual presentations, invited keynotes, roundtable discussions, workshop sessions, and communal events, participants will acknowledge, identify, and challenge pernicious ocean and coastal inequities including past and present events and structural processes at local, regional, and global scales. This will be an intimate gathering of professional scholars and graduate students from around the US, working domestically and internationally, committed to catalyzing just futures in coastal and ocean studies via knowledge and practice sharing, networking, and solidarity building to reaffirm our commitments to changing the culture of ocean and coastal research and policy in a time of fear and retrenchment.

event.title: Lilian Shtereva: taskscapes
event.description: This is a constantly changing exhibit tackling a dwelling perspective through the act of vivification: the moment at which an architectural structure becomes a living residence. Landscape is explored as a perpetual task of moving objects and adapting to an environment that often feels foreign. Space is continuously brought to life and altered by ongoing dwelling and physical work inside and outside of the gallery. Through the ever-growing gesture of collecting materials, and arranging them into a hoard or hoarding structure as temporary shed-like construction. This is an experimental approach to rethink the exhibition space through active rhythms of work, social interaction, and spatial and environmental needs. Visitors are entangled as active contributors and recipients in an ongoing process.

event.title: Our Stories in Motion: A Migrations Exhibit
event.description:
Across Cornell University's libraries - Engineering Library, Olin Library, and Mann Library - view the art, media, and writing of Cornell students and staff who share the ways that migration shapes their lives. The exhibit showcases winning submissions from the Migrations Program's creative writing and art competition and offers interactive ways to share your own own migration story.

Want to share your own story? Tell us about your own migration story with our interactive map. All stories will be anonymous and displayed publicly as part of the Our Stories in Motion exhibit.

event.title: "From the Brink" Exhibit Series
event.location: Multiple locations across Cornell University Library
event.location_name: Multiple locations across Cornell University Library
event.description:
Cornell University Library is hosting a series of exhibits titled From the Brink: Contributions to a Sustainable Future from across Cornell, at different libraries across Cornell University Library and in close partnership with other departments and groups on campus. From the Brink showcases collections, research support, and collaborative efforts across Cornell and illuminate ways of addressing issues of critical, global importance. The series of exhibits aims to stimulate conversations about the threat of environmental and cultural loss and its implications, while also offering insights about positive developments and constructive steps toward a healthier future for our planet and our communities.

 

The series includes: 

Hello, Human! The Emerging Science of Plant Communication and Smart Agriculture

Mann Library | November 6, 2025 – March 20, 2026

 

Music of the Natural World: Cornell Composers on Nature, Ecology, and Climate

Music Library | February 20 – December 23, 2026

 

Last Call: Bird Decline and the Threat of Extinction

Mann Library  | April 16, 2026 – December 24, 2026

 

Going to Gone: Earth's Biodiversity Loss and What We Can Do About It

Mann Library  | April 16, 2026 – December 24, 2026

 

Keeping Common Birds Common: Birds and Habitat at Cornell Botanic Gardens and Beyond

Mann Library |April 16, 2026 – December 24, 2026

 

Weathering the Storm: The Role of Labor in an Era of Climate Change

Kheel Center | October 8, 2026 – August 15, 2027

 

Languages at the Brink: Threatened Languages and How We Protect Them

Kroch Library | October 22, 2026 – May 2027

 

Rivers of Ice: Three Centuries of Glacial Science

Hirshland Exhibition Gallery, Rare and Manuscript Collections | September 17, 2026 – August 27, 2027

event.title: Approaching America: Myth, Dress, and Belonging
event.description:
American fashion constructs a story about who belongs in the national imagination. What is a myth, if not a story worn so often it starts to feel like fact? This exhibition asks what happens when that story confronts its own contradictions: when American myths are pressed up against the labor, land, histories, and people that make them wearable in the first place. Visitors move through the exhibition the way a newcomer might, from idyllic first impressions toward a more complicated understanding of America.

They arrive in search of freedom, clutching onto a dream curated in their mind before they arrive at our front door, passing through the country’s most familiar archetypes—the pioneer, the patriot, the self-made success—before those images complicate and unravel. What emerges is a more contested, more nuanced America than its emblems let on—one stitched with the visitors' own cultures and identities. A complex and ever-changing culture, imbued with stories whispered through the walls as people have come and gone. This exhibition brings together garments selected by different curators to show how American dress expresses, creates, obscures, and ultimately remakes the myths the country tells about itself.

Curatorial Argument: Approaching America reveals how individuals encounter, challenge, and reshape the myths that define America.

Combined Themes 
Made in the USA
Made by whom, under what conditions, and at what cost?
Traditional Americana, national symbols, craft and production, labor, material, industry, and the construction of an “American-made” identity.
Imagining the American Hero
Who gets turned into an American archetype? 
Patriotism, heroism, celebrity and stardom, glamour, aspiration, and the figures through whom American ideals and dreams become visible and wearable.
Redefining the frontier 
Where and what is the “frontier,” and whose history does that mythology depend upon?
Expansion, exploration, reinvention, and the point at which idealized national myths begin to encounter the histories and people they obscure.
Wearing America: A dissenting identity 
Who gets to wear American identity against dominant meanings?
Protest, subcultures, resistance, alternative identities, and dress as a means of challenging the ideals established in the earlier sections.
Self-made 
Who gets to claim self-invention, and what does the myth conceal?
Success, individualism, aspiration, class/mobility, entrepreneurship, but also the possibility of remaking “America” through one’s own identity and experience.

event.title: Fashioning Justice: Ruth Bader Ginsburg ’54 and the Power of Presence
event.room_number: Rachel Hope Doran ‘19 and Terrace Level Display Cases
event.description:
Fashioning Justice: Ruth Bader Ginsburg ’54 and the Power of Presence explores how dress functions as civic infrastructure that shapes belonging, authority, and public life. Grounded in the clothing and accessories of Justice Ginsburg and the worlds she moved through, the exhibition considers dress as signal, shield, and statement. What we wear, carry, and keep can help us navigate public expectations and change them. Moving between intimate personal items and the visual codes of professional power, Fashioning Justice shows how clothing can communicate care, conviction, and resistance through the most subtle details.

This exhibit is a collaboration between the Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy and the College of Human Ecology and is made possible through the generosity of Jeff '79 and Christie Weiss, P'11 and '14.

event.title: Going to Gone: Earth's Biodiversity Loss and What We Can Do About It
event.address: Cornell University Mann Library, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
event.description:
The teeming diversity of life on our Pale Blue Dot—planet Earth—is under grave threat from the impact of our own activity, and biologists are raising the alarm about accelerating rates of decline in the plant and animal species of our world, with sobering implications for the long-term health and well-being of human communities. But if we are the main drivers of biodiversity decline, we also have the power to change the trend.

Organized by Cornell University Library, Going to Gone features illustrations from historical studies of our natural world found in the library’s collections and reflects on the looming possibility of a “Sixth Extinction” on Earth. The exhibit identifies some of the key factors behind the decline of animal species in the 21st century. It also highlights emerging research insights and conservation efforts to give us hope and conviction that preserving the biodiversity of our beautiful planet is within our grasp.

This exhibit is concurrent with related exhibits at Mann Library: Last Call: Bird Decline and the Threat of Extinction, and Keeping Common Birds Common: Birds and Habitat at Cornell Botanic Gardens and Beyond. 

Join us for an opening celebration for these exhibits  on Thursday, April 16, with a lecture by Cornell Lab of Ornithology researcher Jordan Boersma on "Finding Hope in the Search for Lost Birds" at 4:00 p.m. in Mann Room 160, and a reception at 5:00 p.m. in the Mann Library Gallery. All are welcome!

 

Other related events include:

  • “Birds and Blooms” monthly bird and habitat tours, starting April 17 with Cornell Botanic Gardens and the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Register at cornellbotanicgardens.org.

  • “Keeping Our Common Birds Common” hybrid lecture April 26, 3:00 p.m., by Douglas Tallamy, professor of entomology and wildlife ecology in the University of Delaware, presented by Cornell Botanic Gardens, at Call Auditorium, Kennedy Hall by zoom (registration required).

  • Biodiversity Fest, Thursday, September 24:, 11:00 a.m. - 2:00 p.m. in the Mann Library lobby. Come find out about efforts being made by departments, programs and student groups across campus to sustain the diversity of life on planet Earth!

Going to Gone is part of a series of exhibits titled From the Brink: Contributions to a Sustainable Future from across Cornell, hosted by different libraries across Cornell University Library in close partnership with other departments and groups on campus.

event.title: Keeping Common Birds Common: Birds and Habitat at Cornell Botanic Gardens and Beyond
event.address: Cornell University Mann Library, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
event.description:
Organized by Cornell University Library in collaboration with Cornell Botanic Gardens, Keeping Common Birds Common features unforgettable portraits of birds by wildlife photographer Marie Read, taken in biodiverse habitats maintained by the Gardens.

This exhibit shows how managed landscapes that integrate principles of habitat conservation and native plant gardening have a key role to play in protecting and nurturing the beautiful birds that visit our backyards, neighborhoods, parks, fields, and forests, with the hopes of keeping these common birds common forever.

Keeping Common Birds Common is concurrent with related exhibits at Mann Library: Last Call: Bird Decline and the Threat of Extinction and Going to Gone: Earth's Biodiversity Loss and What We Can Do About It.

Join us for an opening celebration for these exhibits  on Thursday, April 16, with a lecture by Cornell Lab of Ornithology researcher Jordan Boersma on "Finding Hope in the Search for Lost Birds" at 4:00 p.m. in Mann Room 160, and a reception at 5:00 p.m. in the Mann Library Gallery. All are welcome!
